title: What will you worship after me
hook: the dying Ya'qub asks his sons, and they answer, your God and the God of your fathers (2:133)
carry: what will you keep after me

segments.voice: Yesterday: the prayer at the foundations, and your line, pray for the ones not born. Ibrahim prayed for his descendants. Today, two generations on, one of them is dying.

At a bedside near the end, the last conversations tend to be short, and about what matters. The mortgage doesn't come up. They ask: are you going to be all right? Will you look after your sister? Do you remember what I taught you? Al-Baqarah takes us into a room like that: an old man, his sons gathered around the bed, and one question. Today: what will you worship after me.
screen: `THE LAST CONVERSATIONS ARE SHORT.` → `AN OLD MAN, HIS SONS AROUND THE BED.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The old man is Ya'qub, Ibrahim's grandson, also called Israel. The verse before says Ibrahim had given his sons a charge, and Ya'qub did the same: God has chosen the religion for you, so don't die except in submission to Him. Then verse one hundred thirty-three asks the listener directly: were you there when death came to Ya'qub? And it lets us in. He says to his sons, in Pickthall's words: “What will ye worship after me?” Not what will you do with the flocks, not who gets what. The one thing he wants to know before he goes. They answer with a chain of names: we will worship your God, the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we submit. Notice one name. Isma'il isn't Ya'qub's father; he's his uncle, the brother of his father Ishaq. The commentators point out that Arabic can count an uncle among the fathers. The sons name both branches of the family in one breath, as one line of faith. In Islamic tradition, a deathbed charge like this has a name: wasiyyah, a counsel, a will. Muslims are encouraged to write a will for their property, and some also leave words for their families about prayer, kindness and keeping ties. Ya'qub's charge was already given. At the very end, he doesn't repeat it. He asks, and lets his sons say it in their own voices.
screen: `WERE YOU THERE WHEN DEATH CAME?` · `WHAT WILL YE WORSHIP AFTER ME?` · `A CHAIN OF NAMES, BOTH BRANCHES` · `WASIYYAH: THE LAST COUNSEL`

segments.voice: Think of someone who will carry something of you after you, a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend, and ask what one thing you hope they keep: not a possession, but a habit, a way of treating people, a word, a faith. Put it into one plain sentence and hold it quietly.
Wasiyyah. A last counsel, a will — Ya'qub's deathbed charge to his sons, asking what they would worship after him. Today's word.
Your line: what will you keep after me. Ya'qub let his sons answer in their own words. Day three hundred forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to prepare a wasiyyah, a will, and some add words of counsel for their families about faith and conduct, following the example of Ibrahim and Ya'qub in al-Baqarah.

chat.says: What did Ya'qub ask his sons as he was dying?
options: What will you worship after me? They named the God of their fathers.
How they would divide his flocks and land fairly among themselves.
Whether they would stay together in the land after he died.
chat.meaning: In 2:133 Ya'qub asks, What will ye worship after me? His sons answer: your God, the God of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, one God.

Ya'qub.meaning: Jacob, Ibrahim's grandson, also called Israel

Ishaq.meaning: Isaac, Ibrahim's son and Ya'qub's father

Isma'il.meaning: Ishmael, Ishaq's brother, so Ya'qub's uncle

sources.quoted: What will ye worship after me?

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:132 (Ibrahim and Ya'qub charge their sons)
Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 2:133 (an uncle counted as a father)

notes: Pickthall's 2:133 question quoted from memory; please confirm.
The uncle-as-father explanation is common in the commentaries (Ibn Kathir cites the hadith 'a man's paternal uncle is like his father'); confirm.
Isma'il described as Ya'qub's uncle (brother of his father Ishaq).
Wasiyyah: Islamic law limits bequests to a third of the estate and fixes heirs' shares; the script only mentions writing a will and leaving counsel.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the old teach said Ya'qub's wasiyyah 'is a single question' and 'he doesn't tell his sons what to keep', which contradicts 2:132, where he gives the charge 'die not save as men who have surrendered'. Teach and fork reveal now say the charge came first and the question at the end. Hook no longer generalizes about what 'people who've sat with someone near the end' say; cut 'like many languages' and 'many also leave words'.
